options.misconception: Airline deregulation came in 1978, under President Carter, and the strike was about federal workers' pay and hours.
options.text: It ended the federal government's role in regulating the airline industry, closing a chapter that began with earlier airline rules.

options.misconception: Reagan did the opposite of bargaining: he gave the strikers a deadline and then fired those who stayed out.
options.text: It showed that the federal government would bargain with any union that threatened to strike against a federal agency.
It signaled a sharp break from the New Deal era, when the federal government had expanded protections for organized labor.

options.misconception: Federal workers never had a legal right to strike; a 1955 law banned strikes by federal employees.
options.text: It restored the right of federal workers to strike, a right that earlier presidents had taken away from them.

rationales.A: Background: airline deregulation came in 1978, under President Carter, and the strike was about federal workers' pay and hours, not airline regulation.
rationales.B: Reagan did the opposite of bargaining: he gave the strikers 48 hours to return, then fired those who stayed out.
rationales.C:
The photograph catches Reagan at the moment he set the terms in public. Background: he gave the strikers 48 hours to return, then fired more than 11,000 controllers who stayed out — a public show that this administration would confront, not accommodate, organized labor.
That is why historians treat the firing as a turning point: the same federal power that had backed unions since the New Deal was now breaking a strike on television.
rationales.D: Background: federal workers never had a legal right to strike; a 1955 law banned strikes by federal employees, so there was no right to restore.
rationales.general:
1. Start with the scene. A president stands in the Rose Garden, in public, to answer a strike by his own government's workers.
2. Ask what he did next. Background: he set a 48-hour deadline, then fired more than 11,000 controllers who stayed out.
3. Ask what changed. For decades the federal government had backed unions; now it was firing strikers on television.
4. Put it together. The firing was a message — to unions, to employers, and to voters — that the rules of American labor politics had changed.
Remember: PATCO was the moment the conservative turn became something workers could feel.
